newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican coffee exports touch record again in Feb.
newsitem.headline: Mexican coffee exports touch record again in Feb.

text.p: Mexico coffee exports, marking a second successive record month in February, are expected to remain strong in March, leaving not that many beans for sale from the 1996-1997 crop, exporters said.

Figures from the Mexican Coffee Council showed the country exported 883,725 60-kg bags in February, topping the previous all-time monthly record for sales abroad of 875,904 bags. That was achieved this January.
Exports in the October-September 1996-1997 cycle to date have totaled 2,634,104 bags compared to the 2,309,881 bags in the same period from the 1995-1996 campaign, a rise of 14 percent.
Exporters reported that the strong export trend has continued unabated this month, with growers and traders animated by relatively strong world prices.
One major Mexican exporter said he expected March exports to be around 700,000 bags, taking the six month cycle export total to around 3.3 million bags.

"Our crop estimate is for 5 million 60-kg bags, we reckon internal consumption will be 900,000 bags and considering carry over from the last cycle of 50,000 bags, that leaves 4,150,000 for export from this crop," he said, requesting anonimity.

He added that 64 percent of exportable coffee had already left the country according to the February figures and if his March prediction panned out it would take the percentage up to 80 percent, leaving 850,000 bags in the country for the final six months of the cycle. "That is not much coffee," he said.

Mexico's internal coffee stocks are at an even lower ebb if other crop estimates are borne in mind. The size of Mexico's harvest is notoriously difficult to predict because of its long time-span and because coffee is grown in so many disparate states at different altitudes.

One recent crop estimate from an executive committee member of the Confederation of Mexican Coffee Growers had this year's harvest dropping to 3.2 to 3.3 million 60-kg bags. Alfredo Moises Ceja said he believed the only state producing more beans this year was Chiapas, with some others seeing drastic reductions.

Such an estimate, one of the most bearish in the sector, would have the country without beans at the end of March and trade talk has already started to speculate about the prospect of Mexico importing coffee.
"I would not discount the import of robustas," said another Mexican exporter, who said local traders have long suspected occasional top-up imports of cheaper robustas from countries such as Ecuador.

"It is done under the table. But with arabica prices so high and Mexico exporting strongly, the rumour mill is already picking up steam. There is a long way to go before 1997-1998 beans are available," he added, also asking to remain anonymous.
Exporters suspect Mexico allowed at least 300,000 bags of robusta imports for internal consumption in the 1995-1996 cycle that went to production of soluble coffee, which is widely drunk in Mexico.

Mexico has limited output of robustas itself. The beans are snapped up cheaply by the major roasters operating in Mexico. Spokesmen for the Association of Coffee Industrialists were not immediately available for comment.
